title: Nicholas of Flüe (1417–1487)
hook: a farmer and father who became a hermit and helped keep Switzerland from civil war

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rita of Cascia, a widow who ended a feud between families. Your line was impossible causes. Did you say the angel's words over something that looked stuck? Day eight hundred thirty-one.

Night, in a narrow gorge in the Swiss mountains. A priest is hurrying down a steep path toward a small cell built against a chapel. Down in the town of Stans, the leaders of the Swiss confederates have been arguing for days, and the talks are falling apart. Some fear the confederates will turn on one another. The priest has come to ask a hermit what to do. The hermit was a farmer, a soldier, a judge and a father before he walked away from his house to live in this gorge. He is still known by a plainer name. Today's word: Nicholas.
screen: `A PRIEST ON A MOUNTAIN PATH.` → `TALKS FALLING APART IN STANS.` → `A HERMIT IN A GORGE.`

segments.voice: Start with the first life. Nicholas was a farmer in central Switzerland, married to Dorothea, and a father. He served as a soldier and sat as a local judge and councilor, and his neighbors trusted him. Next, the hard choice. Later, Nicholas felt called to leave everything and live for God alone. Tradition says he did not go until Dorothea consented. That is not a small detail. The cost fell on her and the children too, and those who honor him honor her. He built a cell in the Ranft gorge, close enough to home that his family could visit. Tradition says he lived there for years taking no food but the Eucharist. People came anyway, for advice. Then, the night at Stans. With the confederates' talks near collapse, the parish priest of Stans went up to Nicholas and carried his counsel back down. The sources don't give his exact words. But the delegates reached an agreement, and the confederation held together. Tradition remembers the hermit's counsel as the turning point. Finally, the name. He is remembered as Brother Klaus, and the Church honors him as patron of Switzerland. In Matthew's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God." Brother Klaus made peace without an army, an office or a vote. He had prayer, a name for honesty, and the trust of people who no longer trusted each other.
screen: `A FARMER, JUDGE AND FATHER.` · `A HERMIT, WITH DOROTHEA'S CONSENT.` · `COUNSEL CARRIED DOWN TO STANS.` · `BLESSED ARE THE PEACEMAKERS.` · then, large: `BROTHER KLAUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one peace. Before the sit, bring to mind one small rift. Two coworkers who won't look at each other. A sibling you haven't called. A neighbor over a fence. A quarrel inside yourself. Let your breathing slow. Don't plan a speech. Ask instead what one honest, simple step would lower the heat by a single degree. If you pray, you can pray the beatitude, blessed are the peacemakers, or ask Brother Klaus's prayers. If you don't, just hold both sides of the rift with the same care. The bell holds the time.
Nicholas. A Swiss farmer and father who became a hermit, and whose counsel, tradition says, helped the confederates make peace. Today's word.
Your line: Brother Klaus. Today, be one quiet go-between: carry a kind word from one person to another who have stopped speaking. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Catholics in Switzerland honor Brother Klaus as their patron, and pilgrims still walk down into the Ranft gorge to pray at his cell and chapel. A short prayer attributed to him, asking God to take away whatever keeps the one praying from God, is still prayed.

notes: Facts to confirm: farmer in Obwalden, married to Dorothea Wyss, large family (index says father; no count stated), soldier, judge and councilor; left with Dorothea's consent; cell in the Ranft near his home; tradition of living on the Eucharist alone; parish priest of Stans (Heini am Grund) carried his counsel to the Diet of Stans; the content of the counsel is not preserved; patron of Switzerland. No dates or counts stated.
'Some fear the confederates will turn on one another' renders the index's 'civil war' cautiously; confirm.
howItsDone describes, does not quote, the prayer attributed to Brother Klaus ('My Lord and my God, take from me...'); confirm.
